title: The Anti-Sniping Agreement: Small Mercies on Sniper Alley
sources: ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), sniping campaign
content:
On 14 August 1994, UNPROFOR brokered an agreement between the warring parties in Sarajevo to cease sniping activities within the city. The accord was a modest, localized measure — one of many attempted ceasefires and confidence-building arrangements negotiated during the siege — but it addressed a form of violence that had come to define Sarajevo's agony in the eyes of the world. The agreement's significance lay not in its effectiveness, which was limited, but in what the sniping campaign itself revealed about the nature of the siege.

Sniping had been a constant feature of life in besieged Sarajevo since the spring of 1992. Positioned in high-rise buildings, on hillside ridgelines, and at key chokepoints throughout the city, snipers from Bosnian Serb forces targeted civilians as they crossed intersections, queued for water, or attempted to move through exposed areas. Certain locations became globally infamous — the stretch of Zmaja od Bosne street known as "Sniper Alley" entered the international vocabulary as a symbol of the city's vulnerability. But sniping was not confined to a single road. It pervaded the city, creating a geography of fear in which every open space, every window, every daily errand carried the risk of sudden death.

The ICTY Galić Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T) examined the sniping campaign against Sarajevo's civilian population in meticulous detail. The trial established that snipers under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps deliberately targeted civilians, including children, in a systematic campaign of terror. The judgment documented individual incidents — a child shot while sledding, a woman killed hanging laundry, a tram full of passengers struck by fire — and placed them within a pattern of conduct that constituted a crime against humanity. General Stanislav Galić, who commanded the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from September 1992 to August 1994, was convicted of terror against the civilian population.

Sniping also occurred from Bosniak-held positions, though the scale and systematic nature differed markedly. ARBiH forces held interior lines within the city, and instances of fire directed at Serb-held suburbs were documented. The anti-sniping agreement nominally applied to all parties.

The August 1994 agreement followed the NATO ultimatum of February 1994, which had established a heavy weapons exclusion zone around Sarajevo after the first Markale marketplace massacre. That ultimatum had reduced — though not eliminated — artillery bombardment. Sniping, however, had continued largely unabated, as it required only small arms positioned in concealed locations and was far harder for international monitors to detect and attribute. UNPROFOR's effort to curtail sniping involved anti-sniping barriers — shipping containers and other obstacles placed at exposed intersections — as well as patrols and observation posts. The August agreement sought to formalize what physical barriers and military presence had only partially achieved.

Compliance was inconsistent. Sniping incidents decreased in the weeks following the agreement but never ceased entirely. The fundamental asymmetry of the siege remained: Bosnian Serb forces held the high ground surrounding the city, and the civilian population below remained exposed. No agreement could change the topography that made Sarajevo a killing ground.

The anti-sniping agreement belongs to a category of measures that characterized the international response to Sarajevo — incremental, well-intentioned, and ultimately insufficient. Each agreement, each exclusion zone, each humanitarian corridor addressed a symptom without confronting the underlying reality that a European capital was under sustained military siege. For Sarajevo's residents, the agreement offered a marginal and temporary reduction in one particular form of daily terror, while the siege itself continued for another year and a half.
